prompt.context: The Canada Oil Sands company recently struck Oil Sands in Canada and are planning to build a production and refining facility. The estimated cost of building a facility is $5 billion and the estimated time for completion is 5 years. The company is concerned about cost and time overruns to complete the project. Five other competitors have already started building production and refining facilities in nearby areas.
prompt.question: You have been hired as a consultant to assess the situation and make the client aware of the potential issues. What factors could lead to cost and time overruns, and how should the company manage them?

clarifying_info.a: Components are fabricated in another country; joining the components and installation take place on-site.

clarifying_info.q: When is labor demand expected to peak?
clarifying_info.a: Peak demand for labor will occur in 3 years from now.

clarifying_info.q: Are competitors facing similar labor demand timing?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — the peak labor demand for competitors in the same region coincides with the client's peak, creating a shortage especially for welders.

framework: Identify potential cost overrun drivers: field profile uncertainty, commodity price changes, environmental regulations, supplier capacity constraints, skilled labor shortage

Identify potential time overrun drivers: design/planning delays, manufacturing lead times, transportation lead times, labor shortage, productivity of untrained labor, government/environmental approvals
Deep-dive on labor (biggest issue): peak welder demand in year 3 coinciding with competitors — explore mitigation strategies
Quantify the financial impact: breakeven analysis without overruns, with overruns, and price sensitivity

questions.prompt: What are the possible reasons for cost overruns on this project?
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure reasons by project phase or input category. Key drivers: (1) uncertainty in field profile raising construction costs, (2) commodity price increases (steel, materials), (3) environmental regulations requiring additional investment, (4) suppliers at full capacity passing investment costs to client, (5) skilled labor shortage — especially welders — driving wages up. Casebook identifies labor shortage as the most critical issue.

questions.prompt: What are the possible reasons for time overruns on this project?
questions.guidance: Candidate should cover: design and field development planning delays, manufacturing lead times for machinery and equipment, transportation lead times, labor shortage during construction/installation/commissioning, poor productivity of untrained labor, government approval delays, environmental authority approvals.

questions.prompt: The peak demand for welders occurs in year 3 and coincides with competitors in the same region. The client cannot get enough welders. What ideas do you have to manage this situation?
questions.guidance: Strong answer covers multiple levers: (1) Automation — automate construction, material movement, fabrication, welding; (2) Pre-welded components — work with supplier to deliver pre-welded parts; (3) Design reduction — redesign components to reduce welding requirements; (4) Shared infrastructure — share piping, storage, etc. with competitors to reduce total construction scope; (5) International labor recruitment — acknowledge barriers: cultural issues, immigration, union opposition in Canada, Alberta climate; (6) US labor recruitment — US manufacturing decline means available skilled welders; (7) Training pipeline — partner with technical institutions to train welders now with guaranteed employment in 3 years.

questions.prompt: Calculate the breakeven number of barrels and years to break even assuming no cost overruns. (Project cost: $5B; production capacity: 100,000 barrels/day; price per barrel: $38; variable production cost: $10/barrel; variable refining cost: $13/barrel; assume 330 operating days/year.)
questions.guidance: Candidate must identify contribution margin per barrel, then divide fixed cost by contribution margin to get breakeven barrels, then convert to years using daily capacity and 330 days/year.

math.setup: Contribution margin per barrel = Price - Variable production cost - Variable refining cost = $38 - $10 - $13 = $15/barrel. Breakeven barrels = Fixed cost / Contribution margin = $5,000,000,000 / $15.
steps: Years to break even = 333,333,333 / 33,000,000 ≈ 10.1 years ≈ 10 years
math.answer: Break-even quantity ≈ 333.3 million barrels; approximately 10 years to break even.

questions.prompt: Now assume cost overruns increase the project cost to $6 billion, with all other variables unchanged. Recalculate the breakeven barrels and years to break even.
questions.guidance: Same approach as previous question but with higher fixed cost. Candidate should note the increase in both breakeven volume and time.

math.setup: Contribution margin per barrel remains $15. Breakeven barrels = $6,000,000,000 / $15.
steps: Years to break even = 400,000,000 / 33,000,000 ≈ 12.1 years ≈ 12 years
math.answer: Break-even quantity = 400 million barrels; approximately 12 years to break even.

questions.prompt: Assume cost overruns push the project cost to $6 billion. If the company still wants to break even within the original 10-year timeframe (333.3 million barrels), what price per barrel of refined crude is required?
questions.guidance: Candidate must solve for price. Breakeven barrels are fixed at 333.3 million (the 10-year target from scenario 1). Set up the equation: Price - $23 = $6B / 333.3M barrels, then solve for Price.

math.setup: Required breakeven barrels = 333,333,333 (same as 10-year scenario). Required contribution margin = $6,000,000,000 / 333,333,333. Price = Required contribution margin + variable costs.
steps: Required contribution margin per barrel = $6,000,000,000 / 333,333,333 = $18 per barrel
Price = contribution margin + variable costs = $18 + $10 + $13 = $41 per barrel
math.answer: Required price per barrel = $41 (up from $38 baseline).

brainstorming.prompt: What ideas do you have to address the shortage of skilled welders that will peak in year 3, coinciding with peak demand from 5 competitors in the same region?

categories.name: Technology & Automation
ideas: Automate welding processes using robotic welders
Automate material movement and fabrication to reduce manual labor needs
Use modular construction techniques that require fewer on-site welds

categories.name: Supply Chain & Design
ideas: Source pre-welded components from overseas suppliers
Redesign components to minimize welding requirements (e.g., use bolted flanges, clamps)
Shift more fabrication work off-site where labor is available

categories.name: Collaboration with Competitors
ideas: Share common infrastructure (piping, storage tanks) with nearby competitors to reduce total welder demand
Joint training programs with competitors to expand the regional labor pool

categories.name: Labor Sourcing
ideas: Recruit welders from the US where manufacturing decline has created a surplus of skilled welders
Recruit from other countries (note barriers: immigration, cultural issues, union opposition in Canada, Alberta climate)
Partner with technical/vocational institutions to train welders now with a guaranteed job offer in 3 years

recommendation: The Canada Oil Sands project is financially viable at the base case ($5B, $38/barrel) with a ~10-year breakeven, but the primary risk is cost and time overruns driven by a regional welder shortage peaking in year 3

The company should immediately pursue a multi-pronged labor strategy: lock in pre-welded component contracts with suppliers, begin robotics/automation investment in welding, and launch a training partnership with technical institutions to build a dedicated workforce by year 3

If cost overruns of ~20% ($6B scenario) materialize, the breakeven extends to ~12 years; the company should either secure pricing contracts at $41+/barrel or seek shared infrastructure agreements with competitors to reduce capital requirements
risks: Oil price decline below $38/barrel erodes the margin that funds breakeven
Welder shortage is unresolved and competitors may lock up the same mitigation levers (pre-welded supply contracts, training institutions)
Regulatory and environmental approvals could add time delays independent of labor solutions
Further cost overruns beyond the $6B scenario are possible given commodity price volatility
next_steps: Immediately assess feasibility and cost of robotic welding automation for the specific construction scope
Issue RFPs to international suppliers for pre-welded modular components
Approach regional technical colleges to structure a 3-year training-to-hire program
Conduct sensitivity analysis on oil price to stress-test breakeven under various price scenarios
Explore formal cost/infrastructure sharing agreements with 1-2 neighboring competitors
